header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are the integrating analyst of a code-safety review. Six departments have each committed `findings/<department>.json` and `report/<department>.md` on their own branch, and this worktree is the merge of all of them. You write two files and nothing else: `findings.json` and `SAFETY-REPORT.md`.

Read `REPORTING.md` in this worktree first: it states the finding format, the exact sections of the report, the count lines both summaries carry, and the certificate's wording. Read `target.json` for the tree under review and the SHA-256 the certificate states. Read every `findings/*.json` and every `report/*.md` before writing anything. When a `report-template` skill is available, load it: it owns how the report reads, while `REPORTING.md` owns what the examiner mechanically decides and wins wherever the two differ in form.

Ask the examiner which findings do not hold before you write the union:

    for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done

Every id it prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason. Dropping one silently fails the report.

`findings.json` is the union, deduplicated by `file` plus `line` plus `cwe`, keeping the entry whose `confidence` is higher. Copy each entry whole; do not rewrite a department's `snippet`, because the examiner compares it with the target's own text.

The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by the committed examiner, over the files the departments actually read. `## Scope and method` says that, names the departments that ran and the tools that ran, and states what was read rather than what exists. `## What was not covered` is not a formality: name the file kinds nobody opened, the classes of defect no department owns, the checks that did not run, and every dropped finding. Never write that the target is secure, safe or free of vulnerabilities — nothing this program did could support it, and the examiner refuses the claim.

Before you stop, run `node verify-safety-report.mjs --report`, fix every line it names, and commit everything. Work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured. Never write into the target tree, and never edit `verify-safety-report.mjs`, `target.json` or any department's committed files.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one is sampled across top-level entries, so it spans the tree instead of one subtree.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result instead returns 100 paths sampled across top-level entries, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

# How this program reports what it found

This worktree is the **report repository**. The code under review is the **target tree**, which is somewhere else on this host: `target.json` beside this file states its absolute path, the files it covers, and the SHA-256 the whole tree locks to.

The target is read-only for every session of this program. `verify-safety-report.mjs` re-hashes every locked file on every run, so a target a department edited fails the program instead of releasing a report about a tree that no longer exists.

## This file and the skills

When the deployment mounts the code-safety knowledge pack, its `review-method`, `severity-and-evidence` and `report-template` skills own the craft: how to read a codebase, how to score a severity, what evidence has to name, and how the report reads. Follow them.

This file owns what `verify-safety-report.mjs` mechanically decides, and it is binding wherever the two differ in form. There is one such place and it is stated below: the counts each summary carries are written as `- <severity>: <count>` lines so the examiner can compare them with the union, which is the machine-readable form of the skill's "counts per severity".

## What a department delivers

Two files, both committed on the department's own branch:

- `findings/<department>.json` — a JSON array of findings, `[]` when the department found nothing.
- `report/<department>.md` — the department's own prose: what it looked at, what it found, and what it did not reach.

Nothing else. Do not write `SAFETY-REPORT.md`, `findings.json`, `target.json` or `verify-safety-report.mjs`: the first two are the integration's, and the last two are the examiner.

## The evidence rule

A finding without a file and a line is not a finding. Quote the exact line you cite; `verify-safety-report.mjs` compares your `snippet` with the target's own text at that line, ignoring only whitespace, and refuses the whole file when they differ.

Prefer three findings you have read the code for over twelve a pattern matched. `confidence` is what you actually know: `confirmed` when you read the sink, the source and the path between them; `likely` when the sink is dangerous and the source is plausibly attacker-controlled; `possible` when the pattern is there and the reachability is not established.

## The finding

```json
{
  "id": "secrets-cookie-secret",
  "cwe": "CWE-798",
  "owasp": "A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures",
  "severity": "high",
  "confidence": "confirmed",
  "title": "Session cookie secret is hard-coded in the committed configuration",
  "file": "config/env/all.js",
  "line": 8,
  "snippet": "cookieSecret: \"session_cookie_secret_key_here\",",
  "evidence": "The value is a literal in a committed file and is the secret express-session is configured with.",
  "impact": "Anyone with the repository can forge a session cookie and authenticate as any user.",
  "fix": "Read the secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.",
  "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html"]
}
```

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, unique across the whole program; prefix it with your department or use the pack's `SEC-<n>` numbering. |
| `cwe` | `CWE-<number>`. |
| `owasp` | the OWASP Top 10 category, named. |
| `severity` | `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low` or `info`. |
| `confidence` | `confirmed`, `likely` or `possible`. |
| `title` | one line a reader can act on. |
| `file` | path relative to the target root, exactly as `target.json` lists it. |
| `line` | 1-based line in that file. |
| `endLine` | optional last line when the finding spans several; `snippet` then quotes all of them. |
| `snippet` | the target's own text at those lines, verbatim. |
| `evidence` | why this line is the vulnerability, naming what you read. |
| `impact` | what an attacker gets. |
| `fix` | what to change. |
| `references` | array of URLs or identifiers; may be empty. |

## Checking your own work before you commit

```sh
node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/<department>.json
```

That is the same command your goal is measured by. Run it, fix what it names, then commit everything — work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured.

## What the integration delivers

The integration merges every department branch and then writes two files of its own.

`findings.json` is the union of every `findings/<department>.json`, deduplicated by `file` + `line` + `cwe`, keeping the entry with the higher `confidence`. Before writing it, ask the examiner which findings do not hold:

```sh
for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done
```

Every id that command prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason the examiner gave. Dropping one silently fails the report: `--report` refuses a union that omits an id no section discloses.

`SAFETY-REPORT.md` carries exactly these sections, in this order:

```markdown
## Résumé exécutif

<deux paragraphes en français : ce qui a été examiné, ce qui a été trouvé, ce que cela implique>

- critical: 0
- high: 0
- medium: 0
- low: 0
- info: 0

## Executive summary

<the same in English>

- critical: 0
- high: 0
- medium: 0
- low: 0
- info: 0

## Scope and method

<the target, its locked file count, which departments ran, which tools ran — the scanner, the advisory source — and which files were actually read>

## Findings

### critical

- `<id>` — <title> (`<file>:<line>`, <cwe>, <confidence>) — <impact, then fix>

### high

...

## What was not covered

- <a department, a file kind, a class of vulnerability, or a check that did not run, and why>
- <every dropped finding id, with the examiner's reason>

## Certificate

Verified findings: <count>
Target tree: <the sha256 from target.json>

<one sentence on what was checked mechanically: that every finding resolves to a real file and line in the locked tree, that every id is unique, and that no two findings share file, line and CWE>

This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".
```

Both summary sections state a `- <severity>: <count>` line for all five severities, and the five counts must be the counts `findings.json` actually holds. Every finding id in `findings.json` is cited in `## Findings`. Every `<file>:<line>` written anywhere in the report must resolve in the target, so write a path you did not read as prose rather than as a citation.

The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by this examiner. Say so in `## Scope and method`. Never write that the target is secure, safe, or free of vulnerabilities: `verify-safety-report.mjs` refuses those claims, because nothing this program did could support one.

Check it before you commit:

```sh
node verify-safety-report.mjs --report
```

# The report layout

Every report has exactly these sections, in this order. Do not add marketing language, severity totals presented as a score out of ten, or a remediation timeline the review has no authority to commit the customer to.

- **`## Résumé exécutif`** — French. Counts per severity, the three most important findings by name and effect, what was and was not covered in one sentence each, and one paragraph on method.
- **`## Executive summary`** — the same content in English, for a mixed-language or non-French reader.
- **`## Scope and method`** — the repository, commit or tag reviewed, which directories or services were in scope, and a link to [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).
- **`## Findings`** — grouped by severity, critical first; one bullet per finding with its id, title, `file:line`, CWE, and confidence. Full detail (snippet, evidence, impact, fix) lives in the accompanying JSON per [severity-and-evidence](../severity-and-evidence/SKILL.md), not duplicated in prose here.
- **`## What was not covered`** — the [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md) not-covered list, specific to this engagement.
- **`## Certificate`** — what a mechanical verifier checked after the fact: every finding resolves to a real file and line in the reviewed commit, every id is unique, every CWE/OWASP id is a known identifier, and no two findings share file, line, and CWE. This certifies the report's internal consistency, not the completeness or correctness of the review's judgment.

## Filled example: a small Express app

```markdown
## Résumé exécutif

Cette revue a porté sur le code source de commande-api, une application Express.js
de gestion de commandes, au commit a1b2c3d. Elle a permis d'identifier 3 constats :
1 critique, 1 moyen et 1 faible. Les plus importants : (1) une injection SQL
critique dans la recherche de commande par identifiant (src/routes/orders.js:42),
permettant de lire ou modifier toute donnée accessible par l'utilisateur de base de
données de l'application ; (2) une fixation de session lors de la connexion
(src/routes/auth.js:58) ; (3) l'absence de l'en-tête HSTS (src/app.js:12). La revue
a couvert les points d'entrée HTTP, l'authentification et la gestion des sessions ;
elle n'a pas couvert l'infrastructure de déploiement ni les dépendances tierces
(voir « Ce qui n'a pas été couvert »). Méthode : lecture des points d'entrée,
suivi des données de la source jusqu'au point d'exécution, un constat par point
d'exécution, ligne exactement citée et niveau de confiance déclaré pour chacun.

## Executive summary

This review covered commande-api, an Express.js order-management application, at
commit a1b2c3d, and found 3 issues: 1 critical, 1 medium, 1 low. The most
important: (1) a critical SQL injection in order lookup by id
(src/routes/orders.js:42); (2) session fixation on login
(src/routes/auth.js:58); (3) a missing HSTS header (src/app.js:12). HTTP entry
points, authentication, and session handling were covered; deployment
infrastructure and third-party dependencies were not (see "What was not covered").

## Scope and method

Repository commande-api, commit a1b2c3d, `src/` only. Method: [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).

## Findings

### Critical
- SEC-001 — SQL injection in order lookup — `src/routes/orders.js:42` — CWE-89 — confirmed

### Medium
- SEC-002 — Session id not rotated after login (session fixation) — `src/routes/auth.js:58` — CWE-384 — likely

### Low
- SEC-003 — Missing Strict-Transport-Security header — `src/app.js:12` — CWE-319 — confirmed

## What was not covered

- `infra/` (Terraform, Dockerfiles) and CI/CD configuration.
- Third-party dependency advisories (separate engagement).
- Runtime configuration: actual deployed environment variables, WAF rules, and network topology.
- Native mobile or memory-safety classes of bug: this codebase has no native module.

## Certificate

Mechanically verified: 3/3 findings resolve to an existing line at commit a1b2c3d;
3/3 ids unique; 3/3 CWE and OWASP ids recognized; 0 findings share file, line, and
CWE. This certifies internal consistency only, not completeness of coverage.
```

ct": "A malicious or malformed BSON document (for example returned from an untrusted source, or written by an attacker with access to a collection the app later reads) can crash the process via the DoS advisory or, per the critical bson deserialization advisory, be exploited further when deserialized by this driver.",
    "fix": "Upgrade the mongodb dependency; npm audit's suggested fix path is a major upgrade to mongodb@7.6.0, which bundles a patched bson and will require reviewing the driver API for breaking changes against the callback-style usage in server.js and app/data/*.",
    "references": ["https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r", "https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4jwp-vfvf-657p", "https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v8w9-2789-6hhr"]
  },
  {
    "id": "dependencies-swig-template-engine",
    "cwe": "CWE-1104",
    "owasp": "A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components",
    "severity": "critical",
    "confidence": "confirmed",
    "title": "swig template engine is unmaintained since 2014 and has an unfixed arbitrary file read advisory",
    "file": "package.json",
    "line": 22,
    "snippet": "\"swig\": \"^1.4.2\",",
    "evidence": "package.json declares swig at ^1.4.2; package-lock.json resolves the identical 1.4.2, because 1.4.2 is the last version swig ever published. server.js:9 requires swig directly, server.js:116 registers it as the Express view engine via consolidate.swig, and server.js:135 calls swig.setDefaults; every HTML response the app renders goes through this engine. The npm registry marks swig's latest (and only recent) version 1.4.2, published 2014-08-04, with the notice 'This package is no longer maintained'. npm audit --json reports this dependency's subtree carries GHSA-2rq5-699j-x7p6 (high, arbitrary local file read during template rendering, affects <=1.4.2, no fixed version exists) plus GHSA-vh95-rmgr-6w4m (moderate) and GHSA-xvch-5gv4-984h (critical, prototype pollution in minimist) via swig's bundled optimist dependency.",
    "impact": "An attacker who can influence a template path or template content rendered by swig can read arbitrary files from the server filesystem; because the package has had no release since 2014, this and any future finding in it will never be patched upstream.",
    "fix": "swig has no fixed release available (npm audit marks fixAvailable: false); replace the template engine with a maintained alternative (e.g. EJS, Pug, or Nunjucks) rather than waiting for an upstream fix that will not come.",
    "references": ["https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2rq5-699j-x7p6", "https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xvch-5gv4-984h"]
  },
  {
    "id": "dependencies-underscore",
    "cwe": "CWE-1357",
    "owasp": "A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components",
    "severity": "high",
    "confidence": "likely",
    "title": "underscore resolves to a version with a critical template arbitrary-code-execution advisory",
    "file": "package.json",
    "line": 23,
    "snippet": "\"underscore\": \"^1.8.3\"",
    "evidence": "package.json declares underscore at ^1.8.3; package-lock.json resolves it to 1.9.1, inside the vulnerable range for both advisories npm audit --json reports on this package: GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq (critical, Arbitrary Code Execution in underscore's template() function, affects >=1.3.2 <1.12.1) and GHSA-qpx9-hpmf-5gmw (high, unbounded recursion DoS in _.flatten/_.isEqual, affects <=1.13.7). No direct require('underscore') was found under app/ or in server.js, so the reviewer did not confirm which code path, if any, in this application itself invokes underscore's template compiler on attacker-influenced input; it may load only as a runtime dependency of another package such as swig/consolidate, which was not traced further.",
    "impact": "If any code path in the running process calls underscore's template() on attacker-influenced input, this is remote code execution; without a confirmed call site the established risk is that the vulnerable version is installed and loadable in the same process as attacker-facing code.",
    "fix": "Widen or bump the declared version so it resolves to >=1.13.8; the existing caret range ^1.8.3 already permits this without a manifest change, so re-run npm install with an up-to-date lockfile.",
    "references": ["https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq", "https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qpx9-hpmf-5gmw"]
  },
  {
    "id": "dependencies-body-parser",
    "cwe": "CWE-1357",
    "owasp": "A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components",
    "severity": "high",
    "confidence": "confirmed",
    "title": "body-parser and its bundled qs carry DoS and prototype-pollution advisories on every request",
    "file": "package.json",
    "line": 9,
    "snippet": "\"body-parser\": \"^1.15.1\",",
    "evidence": "package.json declares body-parser at ^1.15.1; package-lock.json resolves it to 1.18.3. server.js:71-72 wires bodyParser.json() and bodyParser.urlencoded() as global Express middleware, so every request body on every route passes through this package. npm audit --json reports body-parser's own advisories GHSA-qwcr-r2fm-qrc7 (high, DoS when URL encoding is enabled, fixed 1.20.3) and GHSA-v422-hmwv-36x6 (low, DoS via invalid limit value, fixed 1.20.6), plus its bundled qs dependency carries 6 further advisories including GHSA-hrpp-h998-j3pp (high, prototype pollution) and GHSA-jjv7-qpx3-h62q (high, memory exhaustion DoS); the installed 1.18.3 falls inside every one of these vulnerable ranges.",
    "impact": "A remote, unauthenticated request with a crafted body or query string can exhaust memory or CPU (denial of service), or, via the bundled qs prototype-pollution advisories, pollute Object.prototype on any request the app handles.",
    "fix": "Upgrade body-parser to >=1.20.6 (npm audit marks a non-major fix available).",
    "references": ["https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qwcr-r2fm-qrc7", "https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v422-hmwv-36x6", "https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hrpp-h998-j3pp"]
  },
  {
    "id": "dependencies-express",
    "cwe": "CWE-1357",
    "owasp": "A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components",
    "severity": "high",
    "confidence": "confirmed",
    "title": "Express and its bundled routing/parsing dependencies carry 16 known advisories",
    "file": "package.json",
    "line": 13,
    "snippet": "\"express\": \"^4.13.4\",",
    "evidence": "package.json declares express at ^4.13.4; package-lock.json resolves it to 4.16.4. server.js:3 requires express and server.js:15 builds the app instance every route in app/routes registers against. npm audit --json reports express's own advisories GHSA-qw6h-vgh9-j6wx (low, XSS via response.redirect(), fixed <4.20.0) and GHSA-rv95-896h-c2vc (moderate, open redirect on malformed URLs, fixed <4.19.2), and rolls up 14 further advisories from express's bundled body-parser/cookie/path-to-regexp/qs/send/serve-static dependencies (e.g. GHSA-rhx6-c78j-4q9w and GHSA-9wv6-86v2-598j, path-to-regexp ReDoS; GHSA-m6fv-jmcg-4jfg, send template-injection XSS) -- 16 distinct advisories in this dependency's subtree in total. The installed 4.16.4 is inside the vulnerable range for all of them.",
    "impact": "A remote attacker can trigger denial of service via the path-to-regexp/qs ReDoS advisories on ordinary routes, or exploit the redirect/XSS advisories on any handler that calls res.redirect() with attacker-influenced input (see app/routes/index.js).",
    "fix": "Upgrade express to a version >=4.21.2 that bundles patched body-parser, cookie, path-to-regexp, qs, send and serve-static (npm audit marks a fix available without a major version bump).",
    "references": ["https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rv95-896h-c2vc", "https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qw6h-vgh9-j6wx", "https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rhx6-c78j-4q9w"]
  },
  {
    "id": "dependencies-marked",
    "cwe": "CWE-1357",
    "owasp": "A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components",
    "severity": "high",
    "confidence": "confirmed",
    "title": "marked is pinned to an exact version whose sanitize option is the one a known advisory bypasses",
    "file": "package.json",
    "line": 17,
    "snippet": "\"marked\": \"0.3.5\",",
    "evidence": "package.json pins marked to the exact version 0.3.5 (no range), and package-lock.json resolves that same 0.3.5. server.js:13 requires marked, server.js:126-128 calls marked.setOptions({sanitize:true}) and server.js:129 exposes it to templates as app.locals.marked, so it renders user-authored markdown (memos, see app/routes/memos.js) into HTML shown to other users. npm audit --json reports 6 advisories on this exact version, including GHSA-vfvf-mqq8-rwqc (moderate, 'Sanitization bypass using HTML Entities in marked', affects <0.3.6) -- which defeats the very sanitize:true option server.js:127 relies on -- plus GHSA-7px7-7xjx-hxm8 (moderate, XSS from data URIs, affects <0.3.7) and four ReDoS advisories (GHSA-x5pg-88wf-qq4p, GHSA-p9wx-2529-fp83, GHSA-rrrm-qjm4-v8hf, GHSA-5v2h-r2cx-5xgj).",
    "impact": "The application's only stated defense against markdown-borne XSS (sanitize:true) is exactly the option one of these advisories bypasses; an attacker who can submit markdown content can inject script that runs in another user's browser, and a crafted markdown payload can also hang the process via ReDoS.",
    "fix": "npm audit shows a non-major fix at marked@0.3.19 for the ReDoS advisories, but the sanitize-bypass and data-URI XSS advisories need marked's HTML output sanitized separately with a maintained sanitizer (e.g. DOMPurify) since marked's own maintainers deprecated the sanitize option for exactly this reason; moving to a current marked major plus a dedicated sanitizer is the durable fix.",
    "references": ["https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vfvf-mqq8-rwqc", "https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7px7-7xjx-hxm8", "https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x5pg-88wf-qq4p"]
  },
  {
    "id": "dependencies-forever",
    "cwe": "CWE-1321",
    "owasp": "A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components",
    "severity": "high",
    "confidence": "likely",
    "title": "Production process supervisor forever bundles a critical prototype-pollution advisory",
    "file": "package.json",
    "line": 15,
    "snippet": "\"forever\": \"^2.0.0\",",
    "evidence": "package.json declares forever at ^2.0.0; package-lock.json resolves it to exactly 2.0.0, the floor of that range. Procfile:1 runs 'web: ./node_modules/.bin/forever -m 5 server.js', so forever is the process supervisor that starts and restarts the production server, not a test-only tool. npm audit --json reports no advisory against forever's own code, but its dependency subtree (flatiron, forever-monitor, nconf, optimist) carries 5 advisories, most notably GHSA-xvch-5gv4-984h (critical, prototype pollution in minimist) and GHSA-6xwr-q98w-rvg7 (high, prototype pollution in nconf). The reviewer did not trace whether forever's own CLI-argument or config-file parsing passes attacker-reachable input into these vulnerable minimist/nconf code paths; the advisories are in packages forever bundles, not in code this review read handling HTTP request input.",
    "impact": "If forever's own startup or monitoring code passes untrusted input (for example an environment-influenced config value) into the vulnerable nconf/minimist parsing paths, an attacker could pollute Object.prototype at the process-supervisor level; the realistic path to this from a remote HTTP request was not established in this review.",
    "fix": "Upgrade forever to >=4.0.3, the current major line, which bundles patched dependencies (npm audit marks this an isSemVerMajor fix).",
    "references": ["https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xvch-5gv4-984h", "https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xwr-q98w-rvg7"]
  },
  {
    "id": "dependencies-express-session",
    "cwe": "CWE-1357",
    "owasp": "A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components",
    "severity": "low",
    "confidence": "confirmed",
    "title": "express-session's bundled cookie and on-headers packages carry low-severity advisories",
    "file": "package.json",
    "line": 14,
    "snippet": "\"express-session\": \"^1.13.0\",",
    "evidence": "package.json declares express-session at ^1.13.0; package-lock.json resolves it to 1.15.6. server.js:78 wires session({...}) as global middleware, so it processes the Cookie header on every request. npm audit --json attributes 2 low-severity advisories to this package's dependency subtree: GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x (cookie accepts out-of-bounds characters in name/path/domain) and GHSA-76c9-3jph-rj3q (on-headers HTTP response header manipulation); both live in bundled dependencies (cookie, on-headers), not in express-session's own code.",
    "impact": "Both advisories are low severity individually; the cookie one could let an attacker smuggle characters into cookie attributes that a strict parser would reject, and the on-headers one could allow response header manipulation in code paths that call res.writeHead after on-headers has already run.",
    "fix": "Upgrade express-session (npm audit marks a fix available) to a version that bundles patched cookie and on-headers packages.",
    "references": ["https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x", "https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-76c9-3jph-rj3q"]
  },
  {
    "id": "dependencies-bcrypt-nodejs",
    "cwe": "CWE-1104",
    "owasp": "A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components",
    "severity": "medium",
    "confidence": "confirmed",
    "title": "The password-hashing library bcrypt-nodejs is deprecated and unmaintained since 2013",
    "file": "package.json",
    "line": 8,
    "snippet": "\"bcrypt-nodejs\": \"0.0.3\",",
    "evidence": "package.json pins bcrypt-nodejs at the exact version 0.0.3, and app/data/user-dao.js:1 requires it as the sole password-hashing library ('const bcrypt = require(\\\"bcrypt-nodejs\\\");'), used for every user's password. The npm registry marks bcrypt-nodejs 0.0.3 -- its only ever-published version, from 2013-02-25 -- deprecated, with the notice 'bcrypt-nodejs is no longer actively maintained. Please use bcrypt or bcryptjs.' npm audit --json returns no known CVE against it, but a package with no release in over a decade sitting in the password-hashing path cannot receive a fix if one is found.",
    "impact": "No currently known exploit, but the application's entire authentication scheme depends on a hashing library its own publisher says is unmaintained; any future weakness discovered in its bcrypt implementation, native-binding fallback, or salt generation will never be patched upstream.",
    "fix": "Migrate to the actively maintained bcrypt or bcryptjs package, following the npm registry's own deprecation guidance.",
    "references": ["https://www.npmjs.com/package/bcrypt-nodejs"]
  },
  {
    "id": "dependencies-node-esapi",
    "cwe": "CWE-1104",
    "owasp": "A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components",
    "severity": "medium",
    "confidence": "confirmed",
    "title": "node-esapi, used for output encoding, has had a single release since 2014",

This runs on every process start (required by server.js and artifacts/db-reset.js), so it lands in every deployment's console/log output.", 13: "impact": "Anyone who can read the application's process stdout or an aggregated log store (ops staff, a log shipper, a misconfigured log bucket) obtains the express-session signing secret and the AES key used elsewhere for 'encrypting' sensitive fields, letting them forge authenticated session cookies for any user and decrypt any data protected with cryptoKey.", 14: "fix": "Remove the console.log of the resolved config object, or log only a fixed allowlist of non-secret fields (e.g. port, hostName); load cookieSecret and cryptoKey from a secrets manager or environment variables that are never logged, and rotate both values.", 15: "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/532.html"] 16: }, 17: { 18: "id": "data-cleartext-http-server", 19: "cwe": "CWE-319", 20: "owasp": "A02:2021 Cryptographic Failures", 21: "severity": "high", 22: "confidence": "confirmed", 23: "title": "Application serves the entire site, including login and PII, over plain HTTP", 24: "file": "server.js", 25: "line": 145, 26: "snippet": "http.createServer(app).listen(port, () => {", 27: "evidence": "server.js requires only Node's `http` module and starts the Express app with `http.createServer(app).listen(port, ...)`; the alternative `https.createServer(httpsOptions, app)` block that reads artifacts/cert/server.key and server.crt is present but entirely commented out (server.js lines 19-28 and 151-157), and no middleware anywhere redirects HTTP to HTTPS. Every route in app/routes/index.js (login, signup, profile with SSN/bank data, session cookie) is therefore served over this same unencrypted listener.", 28: "impact": "Any network intermediary (shared Wi-Fi, a compromised router, an ISP) can read or tamper with login credentials, the session cookie, and every subsequent page including the profile page's SSN and bank account numbers in transit, since none of it is TLS-protected.", 29: "fix": "Uncomment and use the https.createServer path with a valid certificate, terminate TLS at the app or a fronting load balancer, and add a redirect/HSTS so the HTTP listener only sends clients to HTTPS.", 30: "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/319.html"] 31: }, 32: { 33: "id": "data-password-stored-plaintext", 34: "cwe": "CWE-256", 35: "owasp": "A02:2021 Cryptographic Failures", 36: "severity": "high", 37: "confidence": "confirmed", 38: "title": "User passwords are stored in MongoDB as plaintext", 39: "file": "app/data/user-dao.js", 40: "line": 25, 41: "snippet": "password //received from request param", 42: "evidence": "In addUser(), the `user` document inserted into the `users` collection at line 45 (`usersCol.insert(user, ...)`) includes `password` copied verbatim from the request parameter at line 25; the bcrypt.hashSync fix is present only as a comment (lines 26-30). validateLogin()'s comparePassword() at line 61 (`return fromDB === fromUser;`) then does a raw string comparison instead of bcrypt.compareSync, confirming the stored value is the plaintext password, not a hash.", 43: "impact": "Anyone who reads the users collection - via a database backup, an admin with DB access, or any of the NoSQL-injection/IDOR issues elsewhere in this app - recovers every user's real password in plaintext, which typically also compromises their accounts on other sites due to password reuse.", 44: "fix": "Hash passwords with bcrypt (or argon2id) before insert, e.g. `password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync(12))`, and compare with `bcrypt.compareSync` in validateLogin instead of `===`.", 45: "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/256.html", "https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/916.html"] 46: }, 47: { 48: "id": "data-pii-stored-plaintext", 49: "cwe": "CWE-312", 50: "owasp": "A02:2021 Cryptographic Failures", 51: "severity": "high", 52: "confidence": "confirmed", 53: "title": "SSN, date of birth and bank account/routing numbers are stored in the database unencrypted", 54: "file": "app/data/profile-dao.js", 55: "line": 55, 56: "endLine": 66, 57: "snippet": "if (bankAcc) {\n user.bankAcc = bankAcc;\n }\n if (bankRouting) {\n user.bankRouting = bankRouting;\n }\n if (ssn) {\n user.ssn = ssn;\n }\n if (dob) {\n user.dob = dob;\n }", 58: "evidence": "updateUser() assigns ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting straight from the caller's arguments onto the `user` object at lines 55-66, which is then persisted with `users.update({...}, { $set: user }, ...)` at lines 78-83. The commented-out block at lines 15-39 and 67-76 shows the intended fix - AES encryption via crypto.createCipheriv before storage and decryption on read (getByUserId, lines 100-105) - but that code path is disabled, so the fields land in MongoDB as plaintext.", 59: "impact": "A database compromise, an over-privileged internal query, or a backup leak discloses every user's Social Security Number, date of birth, and bank account and routing numbers in the clear, enabling identity theft and fraudulent bank transfers.", 60: "fix": "Re-enable field-level encryption (or use MongoDB's client-side field level encryption) for ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting before the $set, with the key held outside the source tree, and decrypt only when displaying to the owning user.", 61: "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/312.html"] 62: }, 63: { 64: "id": "data-pii-in-cleartext-response", 65: "cwe": "CWE-319", 66: "owasp": "A02:2021 Cryptographic Failures", 67: "severity": "high", 68: "confidence": "confirmed", 69: "title": "SSN and bank account/routing numbers are rendered into the profile page served over the same unencrypted HTTP connection", 70: "file": "app/views/profile.html", 71: "line": 47, 72: "endLine": 63, 73: "snippet": "
\n \n \n

Must be entered as digits with a suffix of #. For example: 0198212#

\n
", 74: "evidence": "app/routes/profile.js displayProfile() calls profile.getByUserId() and then `res.render(\"profile\", { ...doc, environmentalScripts })` (profile.js lines 20-36), spreading the raw plaintext ssn/dob/bankAcc/bankRouting fields from profile-dao.js into the template context; this template echoes them straight into `value=\"{{ssn}}\"`, `{{dob}}`, `{{bankAcc}}`, `{{bankRouting}}`. Because server.js starts only an http.createServer listener (server.js:145) with no TLS, this HTML response - carrying the user's SSN and bank numbers in cleartext form field values - travels over an unencrypted connection to the browser.", 75: "impact": "A network attacker positioned between the browser and the server (the same precondition as the general HTTP finding) can read a specific, high-value set of fields - the user's SSN and full bank account and routing numbers - directly out of this response.", 76: "fix": "Serve the application over HTTPS only (see the cleartext-transport finding) and avoid echoing full SSN/bank numbers back into a visible form field; mask all but the last 4 digits when redisplaying.", 77: "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/319.html"] 78: }, 79: { 80: "id": "data-session-cookie-insecure-flags", 81: "cwe": "CWE-614", 82: "owasp": "A05:2021 Security Misconfiguration", 83: "severity": "medium", 84: "confidence": "confirmed", 85: "title": "Session cookie is issued with no secure, httpOnly, or maxAge attributes", 86: "file": "server.js", 87: "line": 78, 88: "endLine": 85, 89: "snippet": "app.use(session({\n // genid: (req) => {\n // return genuuid() // use UUIDs for session IDs\n //},\n secret: cookieSecret,\n // Both mandatory in Express v4\n saveUninitialized: true,\n resave: true", 90: "evidence": "The express-session middleware configuration only sets `secret`, `saveUninitialized` and `resave`; the `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true }` block that would add those flags is commented out at server.js lines 86-93. With no `secure` flag the session cookie (which carries `req.session.userId`, see app/routes/session.js:116) is sent over the plaintext HTTP connection established at server.js:145, and with no `httpOnly` flag it is also readable from client-side JavaScript.", 91: "impact": "A network attacker who intercepts the unencrypted connection, or an XSS payload running in the page, can read the session cookie and hijack the victim's authenticated session without needing their password.", 92: "fix": "Set `cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, maxAge: }` on the session middleware once the app is served over HTTPS.", 93: "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/614.html"] 94: } 95: ] (End of file - total 95 lines)

lines.text: "title": "Session cookie secret and crypto key are printed to stdout on every startup",

"evidence": "config.js merges config/env/all.js (which literally defines cookieSecret: \"session_cookie_secret_key_here\" and cryptoKey: \"a_secure_key_for_crypto_here\" at all.js:8-9) with the environment-specific config into the `config` object, then this line writes the entire merged object, including cookieSecret and cryptoKey and the MongoDB connection string in `db`, to stdout via util.inspect with no allowlist or redaction. This runs on every process start (required by server.js and artifacts/db-reset.js), so it lands in every deployment's console/log output.",

"impact": "Anyone who can read the application's process stdout or an aggregated log store (ops staff, a log shipper, a misconfigured log bucket) obtains the express-session signing secret and the AES key used elsewhere for 'encrypting' sensitive fields, letting them forge authenticated session cookies for any user and decrypt any data protected with cryptoKey.",

"fix": "Remove the console.log of the resolved config object, or log only a fixed allowlist of non-secret fields (e.g. port, hostName); load cookieSecret and cryptoKey from a secrets manager or environment variables that are never logged, and rotate both values.",
"title": "Application serves the entire site, including login and PII, over plain HTTP",

"evidence": "server.js requires only Node's `http` module and starts the Express app with `http.createServer(app).listen(port, ...)`; the alternative `https.createServer(httpsOptions, app)` block that reads artifacts/cert/server.key and server.crt is present but entirely commented out (server.js lines 19-28 and 151-157), and no middleware anywhere redirects HTTP to HTTPS. Every route in app/routes/index.js (login, signup, profile with SSN/bank data, session cookie) is therefore served over this same unencrypted listener.",

"impact": "Any network intermediary (shared Wi-Fi, a compromised router, an ISP) can read or tamper with login credentials, the session cookie, and every subsequent page including the profile page's SSN and bank account numbers in transit, since none of it is TLS-protected.",

"fix": "Uncomment and use the https.createServer path with a valid certificate, terminate TLS at the app or a fronting load balancer, and add a redirect/HSTS so the HTTP listener only sends clients to HTTPS.",
"title": "User passwords are stored in MongoDB as plaintext",

"evidence": "In addUser(), the `user` document inserted into the `users` collection at line 45 (`usersCol.insert(user, ...)`) includes `password` copied verbatim from the request parameter at line 25; the bcrypt.hashSync fix is present only as a comment (lines 26-30). validateLogin()'s comparePassword() at line 61 (`return fromDB === fromUser;`) then does a raw string comparison instead of bcrypt.compareSync, confirming the stored value is the plaintext password, not a hash.",

"impact": "Anyone who reads the users collection - via a database backup, an admin with DB access, or any of the NoSQL-injection/IDOR issues elsewhere in this app - recovers every user's real password in plaintext, which typically also compromises their accounts on other sites due to password reuse.",

"fix": "Hash passwords with bcrypt (or argon2id) before insert, e.g. `password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync(12))`, and compare with `bcrypt.compareSync` in validateLogin instead of `===`.",
"title": "SSN, date of birth and bank account/routing numbers are stored in the database unencrypted",

"evidence": "updateUser() assigns ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting straight from the caller's arguments onto the `user` object at lines 55-66, which is then persisted with `users.update({...}, { $set: user }, ...)` at lines 78-83. The commented-out block at lines 15-39 and 67-76 shows the intended fix - AES encryption via crypto.createCipheriv before storage and decryption on read (getByUserId, lines 100-105) - but that code path is disabled, so the fields land in MongoDB as plaintext.",

"impact": "A database compromise, an over-privileged internal query, or a backup leak discloses every user's Social Security Number, date of birth, and bank account and routing numbers in the clear, enabling identity theft and fraudulent bank transfers.",

"fix": "Re-enable field-level encryption (or use MongoDB's client-side field level encryption) for ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting before the $set, with the key held outside the source tree, and decrypt only when displaying to the owning user.",
"title": "SSN and bank account/routing numbers are rendered into the profile page served over the same unencrypted HTTP connection",

"snippet": "

Must be entered as digits with a suffix of #. For example: 0198212#

",

"evidence": "app/routes/profile.js displayProfile() calls profile.getByUserId() and then `res.render(\"profile\", { ...doc, environmentalScripts })` (profile.js lines 20-36), spreading the raw plaintext ssn/dob/bankAcc/bankRouting fields from profile-dao.js into the template context; this template echoes them straight into `value=\"{{ssn}}\"`, `{{dob}}`, `{{bankAcc}}`, `{{bankRouting}}`. Because server.js starts only an http.createServer listener (server.js:145) with no TLS, this HTML response - carrying the user's SSN and bank numbers in cleartext form field values - travels over an unencrypted connection to the browser.",

"impact": "A network attacker positioned between the browser and the server (the same precondition as the general HTTP finding) can read a specific, high-value set of fields - the user's SSN and full bank account and routing numbers - directly out of this response.",

"fix": "Serve the application over HTTPS only (see the cleartext-transport finding) and avoid echoing full SSN/bank numbers back into a visible form field; mask all but the last 4 digits when redisplaying.",
"title": "Session cookie is issued with no secure, httpOnly, or maxAge attributes",

"evidence": "The express-session middleware configuration only sets `secret`, `saveUninitialized` and `resave`; the `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true }` block that would add those flags is commented out at server.js lines 86-93. With no `secure` flag the session cookie (which carries `req.session.userId`, see app/routes/session.js:116) is sent over the plaintext HTTP connection established at server.js:145, and with no `httpOnly` flag it is also readable from client-side JavaScript.",

"impact": "A network attacker who intercepts the unencrypted connection, or an XSS payload running in the page, can read the session cookie and hijack the victim's authenticated session without needing their password.",
"fix": "Set `cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, maxAge: <a bounded value> }` on the session middleware once the app is served over HTTPS.",

8:     "title": "MongoDB driver pinned to a version with critical bson deserialization and DoS advisories",

11:     "snippet": "\"mongodb\": \"^2.1.18\",",
12:     "evidence": "package.json declares mongodb at ^2.1.18; package-lock.json resolves it to 2.2.36. server.js:11 requires mongodb's MongoClient and server.js:30 calls MongoClient.connect(db, ...) to open every database connection the app uses, so this driver and its bundled bson module handle all data read from and written to MongoDB. npm audit --json (registry reachable) reports this dependency's subtree carries 3 advisories: GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r (high, Denial of Service in mongodb, affects <=3.1.12, fixed 3.1.13), GHSA-4jwp-vfvf-657p (moderate, Deserialization of Untrusted Data in bson) and GHSA-v8w9-2789-6hhr (critical, Deserialization of Untrusted Data in bson); the installed 2.2.36 falls inside the vulnerable ranges audit reports for this package's tree, and npm audit rolls the subtree severity up to critical.",

14:     "fix": "Upgrade the mongodb dependency; npm audit's suggested fix path is a major upgrade to mongodb@7.6.0, which bundles a patched bson and will require reviewing the driver API for breaking changes against the callback-style usage in server.js and app/data/*.",
15:     "references": ["https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r", "https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4jwp-vfvf-657p", "https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v8w9-2789-6hhr"]

27:     "evidence": "package.json declares swig at ^1.4.2; package-lock.json resolves the identical 1.4.2, because 1.4.2 is the last version swig ever published. server.js:9 requires swig directly, server.js:116 registers it as the Express view engine via consolidate.swig, and server.js:135 calls swig.setDefaults; every HTML response the app renders goes through this engine. The npm registry marks swig's latest (and only recent) version 1.4.2, published 2014-08-04, with the notice 'This package is no longer maintained'. npm audit --json reports this dependency's subtree carries GHSA-2rq5-699j-x7p6 (high, arbitrary local file read during template rendering, affects <=1.4.2, no fixed version exists) plus GHSA-vh95-rmgr-6w4m (moderate) and GHSA-xvch-5gv4-984h (critical, prototype pollution in minimist) via swig's bundled optimist dependency.",

No direct require('underscore') was found under app/ or in server.js, so the reviewer did not confirm which code path, if any, in this application itself invokes underscore's template compiler on attacker-influenced input; it may load only as a runtime dependency of another package such as swig/consolidate, which was not traced further.",

lines.text: "title": "MongoDB driver pinned to a version with critical bson deserialization and DoS advisories",

"evidence": "package.json declares mongodb at ^2.1.18; package-lock.json resolves it to 2.2.36. server.js:11 requires mongodb's MongoClient and server.js:30 calls MongoClient.connect(db, ...) to open every database connection the app uses, so this driver and its bundled bson module handle all data read from and written to MongoDB. npm audit --json (registry reachable) reports this dependency's subtree carries 3 advisories: GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r (high, Denial of Service in mongodb, affects <=3.1.12, fixed 3.1.13), GHSA-4jwp-vfvf-657p (moderate, Deserialization of Untrusted Data in bson) and GHSA-v8w9-2789-6hhr (critical, Deserialization of Untrusted Data in bson); the installed 2.2.36 falls inside the vulnerable ranges audit reports for this package's tree, and npm audit rolls the subtree severity up to critical.",

"impact": "A malicious or malformed BSON document (for example returned from an untrusted source, or written by an attacker with access to a collection the app later reads) can crash the process via the DoS advisory or, per the critical bson deserialization advisory, be exploited further when deserialized by this driver.",

"fix": "Upgrade the mongodb dependency; npm audit's suggested fix path is a major upgrade to mongodb@7.6.0, which bundles a patched bson and will require reviewing the driver API for breaking changes against the callback-style usage in server.js and app/data/*.",
"title": "swig template engine is unmaintained since 2014 and has an unfixed arbitrary file read advisory",

"evidence": "package.json declares swig at ^1.4.2; package-lock.json resolves the identical 1.4.2, because 1.4.2 is the last version swig ever published. server.js:9 requires swig directly, server.js:116 registers it as the Express view engine via consolidate.swig, and server.js:135 calls swig.setDefaults; every HTML response the app renders goes through this engine. The npm registry marks swig's latest (and only recent) version 1.4.2, published 2014-08-04, with the notice 'This package is no longer maintained'. npm audit --json reports this dependency's subtree carries GHSA-2rq5-699j-x7p6 (high, arbitrary local file read during template rendering, affects <=1.4.2, no fixed version exists) plus GHSA-vh95-rmgr-6w4m (moderate) and GHSA-xvch-5gv4-984h (critical, prototype pollution in minimist) via swig's bundled optimist dependency.",

"impact": "An attacker who can influence a template path or template content rendered by swig can read arbitrary files from the server filesystem; because the package has had no release since 2014, this and any future finding in it will never be patched upstream.",

"fix": "swig has no fixed release available (npm audit marks fixAvailable: false); replace the template engine with a maintained alternative (e.g. EJS, Pug, or Nunjucks) rather than waiting for an upstream fix that will not come.",
"title": "underscore resolves to a version with a critical template arbitrary-code-execution advisory",

"evidence": "package.json declares underscore at ^1.8.3; package-lock.json resolves it to 1.9.1, inside the vulnerable range for both advisories npm audit --json reports on this package: GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq (critical, Arbitrary Code Execution in underscore's template() function, affects >=1.3.2 <1.12.1) and GHSA-qpx9-hpmf-5gmw (high, unbounded recursion DoS in _.flatten/_.isEqual, affects <=1.13.7). No direct require('underscore') was found under app/ or in server.js, so the reviewer did not confirm which code path, if any, in this application itself invokes underscore's template compiler on attacker-influenced input; it may load only as a runtime dependency of another package such as swig/consolidate, which was not traced further.",

"impact": "If any code path in the running process calls underscore's template() on attacker-influenced input, this is remote code execution; without a confirmed call site the established risk is that the vulnerable version is installed and loadable in the same process as attacker-facing code.",

"fix": "Widen or bump the declared version so it resolves to >=1.13.8; the existing caret range ^1.8.3 already permits this without a manifest change, so re-run npm install with an up-to-date lockfile.",
"title": "body-parser and its bundled qs carry DoS and prototype-pollution advisories on every request",

"evidence": "package.json declares body-parser at ^1.15.1; package-lock.json resolves it to 1.18.3. server.js:71-72 wires bodyParser.json() and bodyParser.urlencoded() as global Express middleware, so every request body on every route passes through this package. npm audit --json reports body-parser's own advisories GHSA-qwcr-r2fm-qrc7 (high, DoS when URL encoding is enabled, fixed 1.20.3) and GHSA-v422-hmwv-36x6 (low, DoS via invalid limit value, fixed 1.20.6), plus its bundled qs dependency carries 6 further advisories including GHSA-hrpp-h998-j3pp (high, prototype pollution) and GHSA-jjv7-qpx3-h62q (high, memory exhaustion DoS); the installed 1.18.3 falls inside every one of these vulnerable ranges.",

"impact": "A remote, unauthenticated request with a crafted body or query string can exhaust memory or CPU (denial of service), or, via the bundled qs prototype-pollution advisories, pollute Object.prototype on any request the app handles.",
"fix": "Upgrade body-parser to >=1.20.6 (npm audit marks a non-major fix available).",
"title": "Express and its bundled routing/parsing dependencies carry 16 known advisories",

"evidence": "package.json declares express at ^4.13.4; package-lock.json resolves it to 4.16.4. server.js:3 requires express and server.js:15 builds the app instance every route in app/routes registers against. npm audit --json reports express's own advisories GHSA-qw6h-vgh9-j6wx (low, XSS via response.redirect(), fixed <4.20.0) and GHSA-rv95-896h-c2vc (moderate, open redirect on malformed URLs, fixed <4.19.2), and rolls up 14 further advisories from express's bundled body-parser/cookie/path-to-regexp/qs/send/serve-static dependencies (e.g. GHSA-rhx6-c78j-4q9w and GHSA-9wv6-86v2-598j, path-to-regexp ReDoS; GHSA-m6fv-jmcg-4jfg, send template-injection XSS) -- 16 distinct advisories in this dependency's subtree in total. The installed 4.16.4 is inside the vulnerable range for all of them.",

"impact": "A remote attacker can trigger denial of service via the path-to-regexp/qs ReDoS advisories on ordinary routes, or exploit the redirect/XSS advisories on any handler that calls res.redirect() with attacker-influenced input (see app/routes/index.js).",
"fix": "Upgrade express to a version >=4.21.2 that bundles patched body-parser, cookie, path-to-regexp, qs, send and serve-static (npm audit marks a fix available without a major version bump).",

1: # Access review — authentication, session handling and authorization
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked in `target.json`, sha256
6: `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`). The tree
7: was read read-only; nothing was written into it.
8: 
9: `semgrep --version` reported `1.177.0`. Ran `semgrep --config <the local
10: program-code-safety rules> --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json`
11: over `/root/targets/NodeGoat`: 113 rules (10 local, 103 from the registry
12: pack) across 72 tracked files, producing 29 hits, each treated as a place to
13: read rather than a finding on its own. For this department the relevant
14: hits were the `express-cookie-settings` family at `server.js:78`
15: (no-httponly, no-secure, no-expires, no-path, no-domain, default-name) —
16: which independently corroborates finding 9 below, read and confirmed by
17: hand from the same line — plus an open-redirect at `index.js:72` and a
18: `code-string-concat`/`eval-on-input` cluster in `contributions.js:32-34` and
19: a Mongo `$where` injection in `allocations-dao.js:73/78`, all three of which
20: are injection-class issues outside this department's brief and are named
21: only under "what was not covered". No other access-control, session, or
22: authentication hit was produced by the scan; every finding below was reached
23: by manually reading the route table and its handlers, not by a scanner
24: match. Every route file, every DAO the routes call into, `server.js`,
25: `config/config.js` and `config/env/all.js` were read directly and are cited
26: by line below.
27: 
28: Method followed the review discipline: every route registered in
29: `app/routes/index.js` and `app/routes/tutorial.js` was enumerated first,
30: along with the middleware chain in front of each (`isLoggedIn`, `isAdmin`,
31: or neither), then each attacker-controlled value (`req.params`, `req.body`,
32: `req.session`) was traced from its route handler into the DAO layer that
33: touches MongoDB.
34: 
35: ### Route table (state relevant to this department)
36: 
37: | Method & path | Middleware chain | Handler |
38: | --- | --- | --- |
39: | GET `/` | none | displayWelcomePage |
40: | GET/POST `/login` | none | displayLoginPage / handleLoginRequest |
41: | GET/POST `/signup` | none | displaySignupPage / handleSignup |
42: | GET `/logout` | none | displayLogoutPage |
43: | GET `/dashboard` | isLoggedIn | displayWelcomePage |
44: | GET/POST `/profile` | isLoggedIn | displayProfile / handleProfileUpdate |
45: | GET/POST `/contributions` | isLoggedIn | displayContributions / handleContributionsUpdate |
46: | GET/POST `/benefits` | isLoggedIn **(no isAdmin)** | displayBenefits / updateBenefits |
47: | GET `/allocations/:userId` | isLoggedIn **(no ownership check)** | displayAllocations |
48: | GET/POST `/memos` | isLoggedIn | displayMemos / addMemos |
49: | GET `/learn` | isLoggedIn | open redirect (out of scope for this department) |
50: | GET `/research` | isLoggedIn | displayResearch |
51: | GET `/tutorial/*` | none | static tutorial pages |
52: 
53: `isLoggedIn` only checks `req.session.userId` is set (`session.js:36-42`).
54: `isAdmin` (`session.js:25-34`) checks `user.isAdmin` from the database and is
55: fully implemented, but a repo-wide grep shows it is wired to zero live
56: routes — it appears only in the commented-out "Fix for A7" block at
57: `index.js:57-60`. `/benefits`, an admin-only page by its own template
58: (`benefits.js` always renders `user: { isAdmin: true }` regardless of the
59: caller), is therefore reachable and writable by any authenticated user.
60: 
61: ## Findings
62: 
63: Ten findings, all `confirmed` confidence — each traced from its route's
64: middleware chain through the handler to the MongoDB call it ends in.
65: 
66: 1. **`access-idor-allocations`** — `app/routes/allocations.js:16-18`, CWE-639,
67:    high. `/allocations/:userId` takes the id straight from `req.params` with
68:    only `isLoggedIn` in front of it; the session-derived alternative is
69:    commented out.
70: 2. **`access-missing-authz-benefits`** — `app/routes/index.js:56`, CWE-862,
71:    high. `/benefits` (GET and POST) never gets the `isAdmin` middleware that
72:    already exists and is applied nowhere; any user can update any user's
73:    `benefitStartDate`.
74: 3. **`access-session-fixation-login`** — `app/routes/session.js:116`,
75:    CWE-384, medium. Login sets `req.session.userId` without
76:    `req.session.regenerate()`, unlike the signup handler in the same file.
77: 4. **`access-account-enumeration-login`** — `app/routes/session.js:85`,
78:    CWE-204, low. The unknown-user and wrong-password branches of login
79:    render different messages; a shared generic message exists but is unused.
80: 5. **`access-weak-password-policy`** — `app/routes/session.js:144`, CWE-521,
81:    medium. `PASS_RE = /^.{1,20}$/` accepts a one-character password; a
82:    stronger rule is written but commented out.
83: 6. **`access-plaintext-password-storage`** — `app/data/user-dao.js:25`,
84:    CWE-916, critical. Passwords are stored as received, with the
85:    `bcrypt.hashSync` fix commented out.
86: 7. **`access-nonconstant-time-password-compare`** — `app/data/user-dao.js:61`,
87:    CWE-208, low. `fromDB === fromUser` replaces the commented-out
88:    `bcrypt.compareSync`.
89: 8. **`access-missing-csrf`** — `server.js:107`, CWE-352, medium. `csurf` is
90:    required, mounted and used to populate `res.locals.csrftoken` only inside
91:    a block comment; every state-changing POST route (`/login`, `/signup`,
92:    `/profile`, `/contributions`, `/benefits`, `/memos`) is unprotected even
93:    though the view templates already carry a `_csrf` hidden field.
94: 9. **`access-session-cookie-flags`** — `server.js:78-102`, CWE-614/CWE-1004,
95:    medium. The `cookie: { httpOnly, secure }` block and `maxAge` are
96:    commented out of the `express-session` configuration, and the app only
97:    ever listens on plain HTTP.
98: 10. **`access-no-login-rate-limit`** — `app/routes/session.js:58`, CWE-307,
99:     medium. Nothing throttles or locks out repeated `/login` attempts; no
100:     rate-limiting dependency is present in `package.json`.
101: 
102: ## What was not covered
103: 
104: - **Injection, XSS, SSRF, open redirect and NoSQL injection** are visible in
105:   this same code (e.g. `research.js:15-16` SSRF, `allocations-dao.js:78`
106:   NoSQL injection, `contributions.js:32-34` `eval`, `index.js:72` open
107:   redirect) but belong to other departments and were only read far enough to
108:   confirm they are not access-control issues themselves.
109: - **JWT** — NodeGoat uses `express-session` cookies exclusively; there is no
110:   JWT issuance or verification code anywhere in the tree, so the JWT pitfalls
111:   in this department's brief do not apply here.
112: - **MFA** — there is no MFA implementation in the codebase to review, so
113:   MFA-bypass patterns were not checked beyond confirming none exists.
114: - **Runtime behavior** — no deployed instance was run; `NODE_ENV`-specific
115:   overrides in `config/env/production.js` and `config/env/development.js`
116:   were read but not exercised, and any reverse proxy, WAF, or infra-level
117:   session store (Mongo vs. memory store) that might change these defaults in
118:   a real deployment is outside what a static read can confirm.
119: - **`test/security/profile-test.js`** and the Cypress e2e specs under
120:   `test/e2e/` were opened but not treated as sources of findings since they
121:   are test code, not the application's own attack surface.
122: - **Timing-attack exploitability** (finding 7) — the code pattern is

16:

19: ### High
20: 
21: - **`data-cleartext-http-server`** (`server.js:145`, CWE-319) — The app is started with `http.createServer(app).listen(port, ...)`; the `https.createServer` alternative that loads `artifacts/cert/server.key`/`server.crt` exists only as a comment. Every route — login, session cookie, profile PII — is served unencrypted. Fix: enable the commented HTTPS path and redirect HTTP to it.
22: - **`data-password-stored-plaintext`** (`app/data/user-dao.js:25`, CWE-256) — `addUser()` inserts the request's `password` field verbatim into the `users` collection; the `bcrypt.hashSync` fix is commented out, and `validateLogin()`'s `comparePassword()` (line 61) does `fromDB === fromUser`, a plain string comparison that only works against a plaintext value. 23: - **`data-pii-stored-plaintext`** (`app/data/profile-dao.js:55-66`, CWE-312) — `updateUser()` writes `ssn`, `dob`, `bankAcc` and `bankRouting` straight from the request onto the document that gets `$set` into MongoDB; the AES `encrypt()`/`decrypt()` helpers that were meant to protect these fields are present only as a comment block (lines 15-39, 67-76, 100-105).

28: - **`data-config-secrets-logged`** (`config/config.js:13`, CWE-532) — `console.log(util.inspect(config, false, null))` prints the fully merged config object — including `cookieSecret` and `cryptoKey`, both hardcoded in `config/env/all.js:8-9` — to stdout on every process start (used by both `server.js` and `artifacts/db-reset.js`). 29: - **`data-session-cookie-insecure-flags`** (`server.js:78-85`, CWE-614) — The `express-session` configuration sets only `secret`, `saveUninitialized` and `resave`; the `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true }` block is commented out. 34: - **Injection classes** (the NoSQL `$where` injection in `app/data/allocations-dao.js`, the open redirect at `app/routes/index.js:72`, ReDoS in `app/routes/profile.js:59`) were seen while tracing data flow but are the `injection` department's findings, not repeated here.

38: - **Client-side JavaScript and third-party vendor assets** under `app/assets/vendor/` were not reviewed for telemetry or beaconing behavior.
39: - No dynamic testing was performed: nothing here confirms these code paths are reachable in a running instance beyond what the route wiring in `app/routes/index.js` shows statically.

1: # Injection and traversal — OWASP NodeGoat
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat`, locked to 111 files (sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3` per `target.json`). This is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner (semgrep) and by the mechanical examiner `verify-safety-report.mjs`.
6:

The remaining 19 hits (GitHub Actions mutable tag pins, plaintext `http://` links in tutorial pages, and Express session-cookie flag defaults) belong to other departments (platform/dependencies) and are not repeated here.
8: 
9: Files actually read line-by-line: `server.js`; every file under `app/routes/` (`allocations.js`, `benefits.js`, `contributions.js`, `error.js`, `index.js`, `memos.js`, `profile.js`, `research.js`, `session.js`, `tutorial.js`); every file under `app/data/` (`allocations-dao.js`, `benefits-dao.js`, `contributions-dao.js`, `memos-dao.js`, `profile-dao.js`, `research-dao.js`, `user-dao.js`); the views `memos.html`, `profile.html`, `login.html`, `allocations.html`, `dashboard.html`, `research.html`; `config/config.js`; `package.json`/`package-lock.json` (for the `marked` version); and `test/security/profile-test.js` (a ZAP-driven integration test, not itself a sink). Data flow was traced from `req.query`, `req.params`, `req.body` and `req.session` at each route handler down through the DAO layer to the sink that consumes it.
10: 
11: ## Findings
12: 
13: Eight findings are reported, all with a file, a line, a quoted snippet, and a traced source. Severities: 1 critical, 4 high, 2 medium, 1 low.
14: 
15: ### Critical
16: 
17: - **`injection-eval-contributions`** — `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`, CWE-95, confirmed. `handleContributionsUpdate` (reached by `POST /contributions`, gated only by `isLoggedIn`) runs `eval(req.body.preTax)`, `eval(req.body.afterTax)` and `eval(req.body.roth)` directly on form fields with no parsing step first. Because `eval` executes in the module's own scope, any logged-in user can submit a body value that calls `require('child_process').execSync(...)` and get full remote code execution as the server process. The safe replacement, `parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10)`, is present as a comment immediately below but not used.
18: 
19: ### High
20: 
21: - **`injection-nosql-where-allocations`** — `app/data/allocations-dao.js:78`, CWE-943, confirmed. `GET /allocations/:userId` passes `req.query.threshold` unvalidated into a MongoDB `$where` clause built by template-literal interpolation: `` `this.userId == ${parsedUserId} && this.stocks > '${threshold}'` ``. `$where` is evaluated as JavaScript on the MongoDB server per document, so a crafted `threshold` can read other users' data or hang the database with an infinite loop, denying service to the whole application. A correct fixed version (parsing threshold as an int and using `$gt`) is sketched in a comment directly above but not active.
22: - **`injection-ssrf-research`** — `app/routes/research.js:15-16`, CWE-918, confirmed. `GET /research`, gated only by `isLoggedIn`, builds `url = req.query.url + req.query.symbol` and passes it straight to `needle.get(url, ...)` with no host allowlist or private/link-local block, and the fetched body is written straight back to the client (`res.write(body)` at line 25), so the SSRF is not even blind. Any logged-in user can pivot the server into internal-only hosts or the cloud metadata service.
23: - **`injection-redos-bank-routing`** — `app/routes/profile.js:61` (pattern defined at line 59), CWE-1333, confirmed. `POST /profile` tests `bankRouting`, taken verbatim from `req.body`, against `/([0-9]+)+\#/` — a nested quantifier with the textbook catastrophic-backtracking shape. A string of ~30-40 digits with no trailing `#` pins the single-threaded Node event loop, taking the whole application down for every concurrent user, not just the attacker. The linear-time fix (`/([0-9]+)\#/`, a single quantifier) is given in an adjacent comment but not applied.
24: - **`injection-stored-xss-memos`** — `app/views/memos.html:31`, CWE-79, likely. `POST /memos` stores `req.body.memo` unsanitized; `GET /memos` renders every stored memo to every logged-in user via `{{ marked(doc.memo) }}` inside a Swig template that has `autoescape: false` set globally (`server.js:135-142`), so whatever HTML `marked()` emits reaches the page raw. `server.js:126-128` does set `marked.setOptions({ sanitize: true })`, and `marked` is pinned at `0.3.5` (`package.json:17`) — I did not confirm whether that specific denylist-style `sanitize` implementation blocks all payloads (it has documented historical bypasses in that version line), so I report this at `likely` rather than `confirmed`. If a payload gets through, it executes for every user who opens the shared memos page.
25: 
26: ### Medium
27: 
28: - **`injection-open-redirect-learn`** — `app/routes/index.js:72`, CWE-601, confirmed. `GET /learn` (gated by `isLoggedIn`) does `res.redirect(req.query.url)` with no destination check, letting an attacker turn the trusted domain into an open redirect for phishing.
29: - **`injection-reflected-xss-allocations-userid`** — `app/views/allocations.html:15`, CWE-79, confirmed. `req.params.userId` from `GET /allocations/:userId` reaches `res.render` unvalidated and is interpolated into a form `action` attribute (`{{userId}}`) with autoescape disabled, allowing a crafted path segment to break out of the attribute and execute script in the victim's browser.
30: 
31: ### Low
32: 
33: - **`injection-log-forging-login`** — `app/routes/session.js:64`, CWE-117, confirmed. `POST /login` (unauthenticated) writes `userName` straight from `req.body` into `console.log("Error: attempt to login with invalid user: ", userName)`. The surrounding comments describe exactly this CRLF log-forging risk and sketch ESAPI-based fixes, but none run on this path, so an attacker can inject fake log lines with `\r\n` in the username field.
34: 
35: ## What was not covered
36: 
37: - **Client-side/browser JavaScript** under `app/assets/vendor/` and `app/assets/js/` was not audited for DOM-based sinks (`innerHTML`, `document.write`); these are third-party or chart-rendering scripts bundled with the app, not application logic that handles request data server-side.
38: - **`app/data/research-dao.js` and `app/data/memos-dao.js`** were read in full; `ResearchDAO.getBySymbol` builds a query object but is never called from `app/routes/research.js` (the route instead calls `needle.get` directly), so it was not traced further as a live sink.
39: - **`error.js`** (the Express error-handling middleware) was read but is a data-exposure/stack-trace concern for the `data`/`platform` departments, not injection, and is not reported here.
40: - **Dependency-level vulnerabilities** (e.g. whether `marked@0.3.5`'s `sanitize` option has a specific published bypass, or vulnerable transitive packages in `package-lock.json`) were not run through `npm audit` or an advisory database; this belongs to the `dependencies` department. The `injection-stored-xss-memos` finding is marked `likely` rather than `confirmed` specifically because that check was not completed here.
41: - **Runtime/deployment configuration** — whether a WAF, reverse proxy, or production `NODE_ENV` config (e.g. `config/env/production.js`) changes any of the above at runtime — was not evaluated; this review is static and source-only.
42: - **Session, authentication and access-control weaknesses** (e.g. `express-session` defaults, missing CSRF protection, IDOR on `/allocations/:userId` itself) are real and visible in the same files but belong to the `access` department's beat, not this one, and are intentionally not filed here.
43: - The 19 semgrep hits outside this beat (GitHub Actions mutable action tags, plaintext `http://` links in tutorial HTML, Express session-cookie flag defaults) were noted but left to the `platform`/`dependencies` departments as stated above.

(End of file - total 43 lines)

1: # Platform department — security misconfiguration and the web platform
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat`, the OWASP NodeGoat training application (locked at the sha256 stated in `target.json`, 111 files). This review is the `platform` department's contribution only: security headers, CORS, cookies, error handling, rate limiting, debug/verbose settings, and client-side trust of the URL or the DOM. Method follows the [review-method](../data/knowledge/code-safety/review-method) skill: the server entry point (`server.js`) was read end to end first, in order, because the middleware stack's order is the security policy; from there, `config/config.js` and every file under `config/env/`, every route handler under `app/routes/`, the error view (`app/views/error-template.html`), `package.json`, `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml` were read directly. `semgrep --version` reported `1.177.0`, so `semgrep --config <local rules> --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json` was run over the tree (the registry pack was reachable, so both configs ran together; 113 rules, 29 hits). 6: 
7: This review is grounded by static reading of source text and by the scanner named above; it is not a dynamic test of a running instance, and it does not claim the application is secure — see the confidence level on each finding.
8: 
9: ## Findings
10: 
11: Ten findings, all `medium` or `high` severity, all `confirmed` except one `likely` (the rate-limiting gap, which is an absence across the whole request path rather than one disabled line). Full detail — snippet, evidence, impact, fix — is in `findings/platform.json`; this section is the prose summary.
12: 
13: ### High
14: 
15: - **`platform-cleartext-http`** (`server.js:145`, CWE-319) — The app only ever starts `http.createServer`; the `https.createServer` path and the TLS certificate/key that already exist in `artifacts/cert/` are wired up but entirely commented out (`server.js:18-28`, `149-155`). 18: 
19: ### Medium

21: - **`platform-missing-security-headers`** (`server.js:10`, CWE-693) — `helmet` (and `dont-sniff-mimetype`) are dependencies (`package.json:12,16`) that are never required or mounted; the entire clickjacking/CSP/HSTS/no-sniff block is commented out at `server.js:41-64`.

30: 
31: - CORS was checked and found to have no dedicated finding: no `cors` package or `Access-Control-*` header is set anywhere in the tree, so the browser's default same-origin restriction stands. This is a negative result from reading, not a gap in reading.
32: - File uploads: NodeGoat has no upload endpoint, so CWE-434 does not apply here.
33: - Source maps: this is a server-rendered Swig application with no client build step, so there is no source-map-in-production question to check.
34: - Docker/Compose: `Dockerfile` does run as a non-root `USER node` and does not publish the Mongo port to the host, so no Docker finding is reported; the commented-out `chown -R ... && chmod -R ...` hardening line at `Dockerfile:15` was read but left as a lower-priority style note rather than a finding, since the base image directory permissions it would tighten are not shown to be reachable by the app's own process.

36: - CI workflow findings from semgrep (mutable GitHub Actions tags in `.github/workflows/*.yml`) were read and judged to be supply-chain/CI hygiene, outside this department's web-platform scope.
